title: The rope that was never a snake
hook: a glint in the wet sand at low tide, and a shell that was a shell the whole time
carry: jnana: you are the atman, not the passing mind
tomorrow: the sky over a parking lot goes pale. a Vedic singer saw it too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alvars in a crowded shelter. Bhakti: love for God is its own fruit.
screen: `BHAKTI: LOVE IS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `ROOM FOR ONE MORE.`

segments.voice: Low tide, late afternoon. Something in the wet sand catches the sun and flashes, bright as a dropped coin. It's a shell. Nothing about the shell changed when it was picked up. It was a shell the whole time. What changed was the seeing. Shankara chose very nearly this picture to open his commentary on the Brahma Sutras. Today's summit sit climbs back to the last stretch of the lineage track: jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A GLINT IN THE SAND.` → `ONLY A SHELL.` → `THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Before he comments on a single line of the Brahma Sutras, Shankara writes a preface about that shell: mother-of-pearl taken for silver, one thing mistaken for another. His teaching is that a mistake like this sits at the root of bondage: taking the body and the mind, which come and go, for the self, the atman, which doesn't. Gaudapada, in his verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, gives the same kind of picture. On a dim path, a rope is taken for a snake. The fear is real. The snake isn't. What ends the fear isn't fighting the snake or running from it. It's seeing. When the rope is seen as rope, the snake doesn't leave. It was never there. The Brahma Sutras themselves open with a word that sounds almost casual: now. Now, then, the wish to know Brahman. In his comment on the fourth sutra, Shankara says freedom isn't produced, the way a pot is made from clay. It's what is already so, uncovered, the way the shell was always a shell. Gaudapada's last picture is a firebrand whirled in the dark, drawing circles that aren't there. Hold the stick still, and the circles stop. From up here, jnana looks less like piling up information and more like a light coming on. Ramanuja, whom the year also read, reads it differently: he holds the world and the selves in it as real, the body of God, not a mistake to be seen through. But on the jnana track, the work is this: a bad grade, a mood, a hard week pass across you the way the snake passed across the rope. They aren't you. Look closely enough, and what frightened you turns out to be rope.
screen: `THE SHELL TAKEN FOR SILVER.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `NOW, THEN, THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THE FIREBRAND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `IT WAS ALWAYS ROPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one worry that has been coiled on your path lately, and instead of fighting it, look at it more closely, the way a flashlight would: what exactly is there, and what have you added in the dim light? Stay with plain seeing for a while, then let the worry rest and rest as the one who sees; if you pray, ask for clear sight.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: jnana, the path of knowing, and the rope that was only ever rope. Today's word.
Your line: you are the atman, not the passing mind. Nothing about the shell changed; the seeing did. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta study the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher, and pair the study with reflection and meditation on what the self is.

fork.setup: dusk, a garden path. a coil lies across the stones and your heart jumps. what ends the fear, in Gaudapada's picture?
options: bringing a light and seeing it's a rope.
fork.reveal: seeing ends it. once the rope is seen, the snake doesn't run away. it was never there to begin with.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: jñāna, knowing, the path of knowledge; pronunciation varies by region.

chat.says: bombed a chem quiz and kept saying 'i'm just stupid' all night. nani tapped my head and said 'rope, beta, not snake.' wait, what??
options: Shankara's teaching: you're the atman, not the passing mind. 'stupid' is the snake you added in the dim light.
she means chem is a rope you climb, so study harder and pull yourself up.
she means quizzes are maya, so grades don't count at all.
chat.meaning: In Gaudapada's picture a rope is mistaken for a snake; Shankara says the deepest mistake is taking the passing body and mind for the self, the atman, which a bad grade never touches.

tie.story: Gaudapada told of a rope taken for a snake in dim light, and Shankara said we take the passing mind for the self the same way.
tie.friend: Priya can see 'i'm just stupid' as the snake: one bad quiz passes over her, but it isn't who she is.
tie.you: what passing mood have you been calling 'me' lately?

Shankara.meaning: the teacher whose commentary opens with shell and silver

Gaudapada.meaning: the teacher whose Mandukya verses give the rope and the firebrand

Brahma Sutras.meaning: short teachings on Brahman, opening with the word now

Ramanuja.meaning: a teacher who holds the world and selves real, God's body

atman.meaning: the self, which the body and mind are mistaken for

notes: Summit sit, day 8: revisits 'jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)' (1232–1237) and 'the Mandukya Karika' (1238–1243), with a brief, unranked mention of Ramanuja (1226–1231).

Ramanuja's position summarized in one sentence ('the world and the self as real in their own right'); confirm it is fair to Vishishtadvaita.
